details:
**Josip Broz Tito**
The Communist leader of Yugoslavia from the end of World War II until his death in 1980. He commanded the Partisans during the war, built an independent socialist state, and promoted the slogan "Brotherhood and Unity" to hold together Yugoslavia's many ethnic groups. He is buried in the House of Flowers mausoleum in Belgrade.

**Non-Aligned Movement**
A bloc of countries that refused to side with either the US or the USSR in the Cold War. Yugoslavia was its only European founding member, joining India (Nehru), Egypt (Nasser) and Indonesia (Sukarno). The movement held its first summit in Belgrade in 1961, and Tito became its first secretary-general.

**Tito–Stalin split and expulsion from the Cominform**
In 1948 Tito refused to submit to Stalin's control, and Yugoslavia was expelled from the Cominform, the Soviet-led organization of Communist parties. Tito is said to have written to Stalin: "Stop sending people to kill me... If you don't stop sending killers, I'll send one to Moscow."

**Informbiro period and Goli Otok**
The period of hostility with the Soviet bloc after the 1948 split, lasting until about 1955, named after the Yugoslav term for the Cominform. Suspected pro-Soviet dissidents were sent to the brutal labor camp on the island of Goli Otok in the Adriatic.

**Partisans and Chetniks**
The two main resistance movements in Axis-occupied Yugoslavia during World War II. Tito's Communist Partisans fought both the Axis and the royalist, Serbian-nationalist Chetniks led by Draža Mihailović. At the 1943 Tehran Conference the Allies shifted their support from the Chetniks to the Partisans.

**Ustaše**
The Croatian fascist movement that ran the Nazi puppet Independent State of Croatia during World War II and carried out mass murders of Serbs, Jews and Roma. Many Ustaše and other collaborators who fled to Austria in 1945 were killed after being sent back in the Bleiburg repatriations. Archbishop Aloysius Stepinac was later convicted of collaboration in a heavily criticized show trial.

**Slobodan Milošević and the breakup of Yugoslavia**
The Serbian nationalist leader who rose to power in the late 1980s, including with a 1989 speech on the 600th anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo. He presided over the violent breakup of the country in the 1990s (the Yugoslav Wars) and was toppled in the 2000 "Bulldozer Revolution." He died in The Hague in 2006 while on trial for war crimes and genocide before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY).

**Operation Allied Force and the Chinese embassy bombing**
NATO's 1999 bombing campaign against Yugoslavia during the Kosovo War, launched after the Rambouillet talks failed. A US strike accidentally hit the Chinese embassy in Belgrade, killing three journalists and sparking protests in China; CIA director George Tenet testified that the intended target was an arms depot.

**Corfu Declaration and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes**
The 1917 agreement between Serbia's government-in-exile and the Yugoslav Committee that led to a joint South Slavic kingdom in 1918. Its original name was the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes; it was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929.

**Alexander I and the January 6th Dictatorship**
The first Yugoslav king, who abolished the constitution and imposed royal dictatorship on January 6, 1929. He was assassinated in Marseille in 1934 by Vlado Chernozemski of the Macedonian revolutionary group IMRO, working with the Ustaše.

**Peter II**
Alexander I's son, who became king at age 11 in 1934 under the regency of Prince Paul. Paul joined the Axis in 1941, a coup then put Peter on the throne, and Germany invaded soon after. Peter's government-in-exile reached the Treaty of Vis with Tito, but Peter was formally deposed in November 1945 when the monarchy was abolished.

**Workers' self-management**
The distinctive Yugoslav model of socialism, in which workers' councils, rather than central state planners, ran enterprises, and local government was organized in communes (opštine). Yugoslavia was also home to the humanist Marxist "Praxis School" of philosophers.

**Ten-Day War**
The brief 1991 conflict in which Slovenia won its independence from the Yugoslav People's Army. It was the first of the Yugoslav Wars and was partly provoked by the JBTZ trial of Slovene journalists who had criticized the army.

**Bosnian War, Srebrenica and the Dayton Accords**
The 1992–95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina included the siege of Sarajevo and the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys by Bosnian Serb forces. The Dayton Accords ended the war and contain Bosnia's current constitution.

**Kosovo War**
The 1998–99 conflict between Milošević's forces and the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) in the province of Kosovo, whose capital is Pristina. It ended with NATO intervention and the Kumanovo Agreement.
